paragraphs: Scope: this page covers only O*NET-SOC 51-4061.00, Model Makers, Metal and Plastic, for career exploration. It excludes wood modelmaking, pattern forming, die and mold making, and ordinary batch machining, and does not authorize machine tool operation, CNC programming, or safety work.

How to assess: use an entirely fictional two-dimensional drawing and dimension table to check whether you can sequence machining operations, choose measuring instruments, record three measurements and tolerance decisions, and explain rework decisions. Perform paper exercises only; do not use powered machine tools.

Who it suits: people willing to interpret drawings into dimensions and operations, repeat measurements and rework, notice small errors, operate tools steadily, and stop equipment to seek verification when dimensions are abnormal or equipment is uncertain. These are behavioral signals, not personality diagnoses.

Note: personality labels and interest codes cannot determine fit or qualifications. Exercises on this page do not authorize machine tool operation, CNC programming, lifting, or safety work and do not use real equipment, employer drawings, or production data.

entries: Drawing interpretation and process planning: study drawings, sketches, and three-dimensional data to determine materials, dimensions, tolerances, datums, and machining sequences.
Machine tool setup and programming: clamp and align workpieces, set tools, set up general-purpose machine tools, or write and call CNC programs.
Machining to shape: turn, mill, drill, grind, and otherwise machine metal or plastic blanks to specified dimensions and shapes.
Assembly and fit: drill, tap, ream, and assemble parts and components, and verify fit and function.
Precision measurement and rework: use precision instruments to verify dimensions and geometric tolerances, rework out-of-tolerance areas or adjust programs, and measure again.
Records and handover: document dimensions, program versions, deviations, and rework decisions, and hand over to engineering and responsible personnel.

paragraphs: The core value of metal and plastic modelmakers is turning drawings into measurable physical objects. Starting from drawings, materials, and tolerance requirements, they plan operations, set up or program machine tools, machine shapes, assemble, measure precisely, and rework to deliver working models or prototypes for engineering verification.

Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 98% of respondents wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 73% stand continually or almost continually, 62% continually use their hands to operate tools and workpieces, 49% encounter contaminants daily, and 70% work more than 40 hours per week.

Capability priorities: extract materials, dimensions, and tolerances from drawings, sequence operations and set up or program machine tools, skillfully verify results with measuring instruments, and stop equipment to seek verification when anomalies arise. Requires machining, CNC, and measurement knowledge and a habit of retaining records according to procedures.

Occupational judgments: key decisions concern whether tolerances can be met, clamping and operations are appropriate, dimensions are out of tolerance, and models can pass engineering verification. Stop equipment and escalate first when uncertain or beyond authorization.

Main outputs: measurable working models or prototypes, machining operation and program records, dimensional measurement and rework records, and deliverable workpieces meeting drawing and tolerance requirements.

Work environment: mainly machine shops and prototype workshops, often paced by projects and orders. 69% of respondents work indoors in environmentally controlled conditions daily, and 36% report never encountering hazardous equipment. Protection is nevertheless needed against flying chips, sharp edges, noise, and metalworking fluid contact.

Complete work cycle: interpret drawings and technical information, plan operations and tooling, set up and program machine tools, machine shapes, measure precisely, rework and adjust, and record and hand over. Each step requires verifiable evidence.

Choose directions based on actual tasks and verifiable evidence. Metal and plastic modelmakers focus on turning drawings into physical working models; wood modelmakers use different materials, machinists focus more on producing parts to established drawings, and tool and die makers bear more comprehensive responsibility for production tooling.
Comparisons use official O*NET 51-4061.00 and adjacent occupation task and work context descriptions. Similar titles do not make duties, qualifications, and safety authorizations interchangeable.

Adjacent directions support comparisons of task objects, outputs, and responsibility boundaries only, not job recommendations. Check individually who diagnoses, machines, measures, and signs releases.

Difference from Model Makers, Wood: wood modelmaking primarily shapes wood using woodworking machinery and templates; this occupation primarily cuts metal and machines plastic parts, with different tooling, cutting tools, and measuring instruments.
If you prefer stable production of parts to established drawings, compare Machinists; if you want full responsibility for production tooling quality, compare Tool and Die Makers.

Current modelmakers: use tools for low-risk steps such as draft drawing and operation checklists and measurement record organization, while retaining human review, first-article checks, and shutdown for anomalies.

Practice drawing interpretation, measuring instrument use, and safety procedures first, then verify through simulation or offline programs. Do not operate machine tools based directly on tool outputs.
Apprentices and newcomers: use tools for low-risk steps such as draft drawing and operation checklists and measurement record organization, while retaining human review and shutdown for anomalies.
Practice drawing interpretation, measuring instrument use, and safety procedures first, then verify through simulation or offline programs. Do not treat tool outputs as process conclusions.
Shop supervisors and process personnel: establish review points for program versions, toolpaths, and first-article inspection, and specify who signs dimensional decisions and quality conclusions.
Include program versions, tool offsets, and first-article decisions in process controls; handle anomalies according to shutdown and escalation rules.

Career changers: demonstrate drawing interpretation, measurement, and rework capabilities through verifiable practice pieces and dimension records; do not treat tool-generated content as evidence of capability.
Develop machining and measurement fundamentals first, then accumulate workpieces and records through public or simulated projects.

Insufficient evidence: a national occupational wage distribution in mainland China matching O*NET-SOC 51-4061.00 has not been obtained. National Bureau of Statistics manufacturing and production/manufacturing job groups may serve as matching references, not wages for this occupation or an individual.

In 2025, average annual wages of manufacturing employees in mainland China's urban non-private units were 113,594 yuan/year (National Bureau of Statistics definition, nominal growth 5.2%). This is an industry proxy, not exact occupational wages.

In 2025, average annual wages for production, manufacturing, and related personnel in enterprises above designated size were 80,739 yuan/year (nominal growth 2.8%); manufacturing wages in urban private units were 76,055 yuan/year. Different statistical populations cannot be combined into a range.

Actual compensation also depends on region, machine tool type (general-purpose or CNC), product industry, shifts, and experience. Check published conditions for specific cities, employers, and job levels.
This is the 2025 BLS OEWS national median, not a starting wage, senior role wage, or individual offer, and it cannot be converted into individual earnings in mainland China.
Percentiles and medians use 2025 BLS OEWS national definitions and cannot be directly compared across years, regions, or occupations.
Percentiles do not divide newcomers from managers. Paid hours and working arrangements vary by employer and project.
Low percentiles are not starting wages, and distribution data cannot be used to calculate individual take-home or after-tax earnings.
Verify actual compensation by specific employer, region, and job level; do not treat aggregate statistics as individual wage promises.
Official percentiles follow statistical definitions and cannot establish individual monthly earnings, full-year earnings, or starting wages.

entries: Realistic: prefers hands-on work with machine tools, tools, and workpieces, gaining feedback from physical machining.
Verify through real workpieces and dimension records rather than labels.
Conventional: prefers handling data, records, and versions according to procedures and tolerance standards.
Use process diagrams and recordkeeping standards as observation subjects.
Conscientiousness tendency: willing to repeat measurement, review, and rework until tolerances are met.
Measure through verifiable dimension records rather than self-evaluation.
Stability and fine manipulation: can remain steady during prolonged standing and repetitive machining.
Use low-risk exercises to observe hand steadiness and sustained attention.
Spatial visualization: can infer part shapes and assembly relationships from drawings or three-dimensional data.
Use shape judgment questions based on fictional drawings for a low-cost experience.
Safety and procedural awareness: willing to wear protection, follow shutdown and isolation rules, and escalate anomalies.
Use compliance during safety drills as an observation indicator.

paragraphs: O*NET lists the interest code RC (Realistic + Conventional), which describes activity preferences only and cannot establish hiring, competence, or safety qualifications.
Exploratory tool, not qualification or hiring evidence.

This checklist is an editorial synthesis and cannot replace employer safety procedures, machine tool operating procedures, or local regulations. Specific protection, exposure limits, and authorization depend on relevant authority and employer documents.

The most important issues to assess in advance are contact risks from rotating and moving machine parts, chip and sharp-edge handling, and metalworking fluid exposure. Exposure points differ across general-purpose machine tools, CNC machining, and deburring and finishing.

Evidence scope: machine guarding references U.S. OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart O; metalworking fluid health effects reference CDC/NIOSH publications. Work context percentages reflect U.S. O*NET respondents and are not extrapolated to other regions.
Affected roles and tasks: personnel using lathes, milling machines, drill presses, grinders, and similar equipment for clamping, cutting, and cleaning.
Potential consequences: entanglement, cuts, eye injuries, or scrapped workpieces, with downtime potentially affecting project schedules.
Qualification and training requirements depend on employer and local rules. The paths on this page are editorial syntheses, not standardized job levels or promotion promises.
Can interpret drawings and tolerances under guidance, correctly use measuring instruments and general-purpose machine tools to complete simple parts, and self-inspect.

Can independently plan operations, set up or program CNC machine tools, complete model parts with tolerance requirements, and review according to recordkeeping standards.

Can handle complex shapes and fits, design tooling and fixtures, and lead first-article inspection and deviation analysis.
Complex models and tooling
Can lead process standards, quality improvement, and mentoring within authorization, without replacing employer safety and quality sign-off responsibilities.

method_cards.含义: CAD/CAM, CNC programming, and simulation may assist drawing checks, draft toolpaths and programs, and measurement data organization. Producing a conforming physical object still depends on machine tools, clamping, cutting tools, and human judgment.

Software mentions in recruitment and O*NET Hot Technologies indicate common work environments and technical requirements only, such as PTC Creo Parametric, Mastercam, and Excel. They do not establish that all roles run automatically or that people have been replaced.

Insufficient evidence: causal research on generative AI adoption, efficiency gains, or job changes in this occupation has not been obtained. Prototyping, assembly, measurement, rework, and safety control are existing occupational tasks. Global exposure studies cannot establish how this occupation is more likely to change.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work pressures, risks, and boundaries for modelmakers

risks.mitigation: Use guards and interlocks, remove chips after shutdown, wear appropriate PPE, and receive training
risks.scenario: Clamping and machining on lathes, milling machines, drill presses, or grinders without protection, or removing chips before shutdown
risks.title: Machine tool entanglement and flying chips

risks.consequence: May cut hands or scratch and scrap workpieces
risks.mitigation: After shutdown and isolation according to equipment procedures, handle sharp edges using fixtures and deburring tools. Select cut-resistant gloves only for stationary workpiece tasks according to employer risk assessments; do not wear gloves that could become entangled near rotating parts.
risks.scenario: Holding workpieces by hand in direct contact with sharp edges while deburring or chamfering
risks.title: Sharp edges and burrs

risks.affected_roles: Personnel operating machine tools with cutting fluids
risks.consequence: Associated with skin and respiratory health problems
risks.mitigation: Ventilation and fluid tank maintenance, protective equipment, and exposure monitoring
risks.scenario: Prolonged contact with cutting fluid mist, splashes, or contaminated surfaces with poor ventilation
risks.title: Metalworking fluid contact

risks.consequence: May scrap entire parts, require rework, or affect engineering verification conclusions
risks.mitigation: Complete first-article inspection, instrument calibration, and program version verification before continuing machining
risks.scenario: Reading or tool setting errors, or unverified program versions, cause critical dimensions to exceed tolerances
risks.title: Dimensions outside tolerances

risks.affected_roles: Programming and machine tool operation personnel
risks.consequence: May damage machine tools, cutting tools, or workpieces and cause downtime
risks.mitigation: Simulation and dry-run validation, single-block execution, and authorization confirmation
risks.scenario: Running programs with incorrect coordinates, tool offsets, or safe heights
risks.title: Program or toolpath errors causing tool collisions

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for dimension records and handovers
risks.consequence: Difficult to establish compliance with dimensional requirements or trace changes
risks.mitigation: Measure again according to recordkeeping standards and retain versions and deviations
risks.scenario: Failing to record measured values, program versions, or rework decisions
risks.title: Incomplete measurement and records

components.definition_block: Metal and plastic modelmakers (O*NET-SOC 51-4061.00, Model Makers, Metal and Plastic) set up and operate lathes, milling machines, engraving machines, jig borers, and other machine tools to make metal or plastic working models and prototypes according to drawings, including template makers.

fermat_decision_card.summary: Suits people willing to interpret drawings into dimensions and operations, repeat measurements and rework, notice small errors, operate tools steadily, and stop equipment to seek verification when dimensions are abnormal or equipment is uncertain.
fermat_decision_card.title: What kinds of people are suited to modelmaking?

hero.quick_answer: Metal and plastic modelmakers set up and operate lathes, milling machines, engraving machines, jig borers, and other machine tools to turn drawing, tolerance, and material requirements into inspectable working models or prototypes. Core actions are interpreting drawings and sequencing operations, machine tool setup and CNC programming, machining to shape, precision measurement, reworking deviations, and retaining dimension records.

description.text: Metal and plastic modelmakers set up and operate machine tools according to drawings to produce measurable working models and prototypes. This page explains task scope, U.S. BLS 2025 wages and employment, Chinese industry proxy wages, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry paths.

subject.name: Modelmakers
subject.summary: Metal and plastic modelmakers (O*NET 51-4061.00, Model Makers, Metal and Plastic) set up and operate lathes, milling machines, engraving machines, jig borers, and other machine tools to produce metal or plastic working models and prototypes according to drawings. The scope includes template makers but excludes wood modelmakers, die and mold making, pattern forming, and ordinary batch machining.
